title: North Korea Fires a Ballistic Missile After Kim Yo-jong Rejects Dialogue as Seoul Demands an Apology, While Ethiopia and Eritrea Sever All Ties and Saudi Arabia Prepares a 100,000-Troop Offensive Against the Houthis
subhead: Pyongyang's first weapons launch in nearly two weeks lands on a deepening DMZ landmine dispute, while the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea both move toward open war — three separate fronts where de-escalation is losing ground.

sections.heading: North Korea Launches a Missile as the DMZ Row Escalates
sections.body:
North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward the East Sea on Saturday, according to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, which said the missile flew roughly 700 kilometers after launch from the Wonsan area — a distance consistent with a medium-range system (Yonhap, Korea Herald, AP). US Pacific Command confirmed the launch, saying it was consulting with allies and that the event posed no immediate threat to US personnel or territory.

The launch comes three days after Seoul demanded an apology from Pyongyang over a mine explosion at the Demilitarized Zone that injured South Korean soldiers, and one day after Kim Yo-jong, the North Korean leader's sister, publicly dismissed any prospect of inter-Korean dialogue (Yonhap). South Korea's presidential office convened an emergency security meeting in response. The salvo is the first North Korean ballistic launch in about 13 days, breaking a short lull that had followed weeks of heightened peninsula tension.
sections.whyItMatters: Pyongyang is answering Seoul's apology demand with a missile rather than a concession. That closes the door on the brief diplomatic opening and re-anchors the peninsula in the tit-for-tat cycle, with Washington's attention pulled toward the Gulf and the US midterms.

sections.heading: Ethiopia and Eritrea Cut Diplomatic Ties as the Tigray War Widens
sections.body:
Ethiopia and Eritrea severed diplomatic relations after Addis Ababa said it would shut its embassy in Asmara and declared 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata — a tit-for-tat that Eritrea mirrored (Al Jazeera, BBC, Reuters via DAWN). The rupture follows the resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia roughly a week ago; more than 50 people have been killed since combat restarted, per the BBC.

On the ground, militiamen allied with Ethiopia's federal government said they were advancing on Mekelle, the Tigray regional capital, raising fears of a wider war (Reuters via DAWN, Al-Monitor). The Tigray conflict is no longer a purely domestic affair: as Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt trade accusations, the African Union has been drawn in, and reports have circulated that militarized commercial drones have reached Addis Ababa's airspace (DW, The Africa Report).
sections.whyItMatters: The Ethiopia-Eritrea break-up revives the 1998-2000 war dynamic between the two, in a region that never fully settled its post-2022 peace. It also pulls Egypt in through the Nile and Red Sea files, turning the Horn into a multi-sided arena at the moment global attention is fixed on the Gulf.

sections.heading: Saudi Arabia Prepares a 100,000-Troop Push to Break the Houthi Chokehold on the Red Sea
sections.body:
Saudi Arabia is weighing a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis to push them away from the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, with options including a coastal drive to protect shipping lanes or synchronized attacks across Yemen (Reuters, Axios, Ynet). Ynet reported that Riyadh is planning an operation involving up to 100,000 troops, with Yemeni forces fighting on the ground under Saudi air cover; Reuters cited regional and Western officials saying the operation could launch in the coming weeks.

Crucially, the US will not join the campaign 'for now,' according to Axios. The Houthis seized the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint in September and have disrupted Red Sea traffic since, astride the world's fourth-most-important shipping corridor. The planned operation would be the largest Saudi military undertaking in Yemen in years.
sections.whyItMatters: A land campaign over the Red Sea's southern gate is a far bigger commitment than the airstrikes Riyadh has relied on for years. With Washington standing aside, Saudi Arabia would be testing whether it can re-establish deterrence on its own — and the outcome will decide whether one of the planet's key trade arteries stays contested.

sections.heading: China and Japan Slide Toward the Worst Split in Decades, and the US Puts New Missiles Next to Taiwan
sections.body:
Chinese state media has dropped Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's official title and now refers to her by name, a pointed diplomatic downgrade amid the deepening rift over Taiwan (SBS). China's top diplomat separately said relations with Japan needed 'normalization' again, describing ties as being at a low not seen in decades (Bloomberg via BusinessMirror). The estrangement stems from Takaichi's comments on a Taiwan contingency and Beijing's retaliatory export controls on dual-use goods for Japan's military.

In parallel, the US military will deploy the NMESIS anti-ship missile launcher to Yonaguni, Japan's westernmost island about 110 kilometers from Taiwan, for the first time during this month's Keen Sword joint exercises, according to Japanese and defense sources (Japan Times, TASS, Iwagate Nippo). The deployment involves no live fire but is explicitly aimed at deterring Chinese maritime expansion. Beijing's Global Times warned it increases the security risk if Tokyo intervenes in the Taiwan question. Taiwan separately took delivery of its first two F-16Vs.
sections.whyItMatters: Two tracks are converging: a diplomatic freeze between Asia's second- and third-largest economies, and the forward basing of US anti-ship missiles on islands that would be on the front line of any Taiwan contingency. Tokyo's willingness to host them, days after China named-and-shamed its prime minister, makes the Taiwan issue a domestic political dispute between Japan and China, not just a cross-Strait one.

sections.heading: Europe Plans a Defence Union as Italy Becomes the First Ally to Cut its Military Budget
sections.body:
Documents seen by The Irish Times reveal the extent of plans for a new European 'defence union,' with capitals encouraging moves toward a common 'European defence culture' and closer NATO cooperation. The push is real but under strain: Europe's roughly €1.2-trillion rearmament drive risks wasting billions through fragmented national spending, analysts warn (InView).

The first political casualty appeared in Rome. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's coalition agreed to scale back a planned defence-spending hike by up to €8 billion, cutting military funding from a projected €21-22 billion to around €14 billion — a concession to Matteo Salvini's League, driven by war fatigue and inflation (Reuters, Defense News, la Repubblica). Italy will still seek EU budget flexibility for energy and defence, but the retreat is the first clear sign that the rearmament consensus is colliding with domestic fiscal politics.
sections.whyItMatters: European officials are signaling a stronger European pillar inside NATO, but Italy's cut shows the money may not follow the rhetoric. If the largest EU defence spenders trim budgets while the US pushes allies to carry more of the load, the gap between the alliance's stated plans and its actual force generation widens.

sections.heading: The US and Australia Suspend Consular Services in Brazil Days Before a Pivotal Election
sections.body:
The United States suspended consular services in Brazil and Australia's embassy temporarily closed, both citing security concerns, just ahead of Brazilian election day (Al Jazeera, Washington Post, Reuters via Straits Times). The closures came as President Lula da Silva, running for re-election, and his rival were in the final stretch of the campaign. US officials described the move as raising tensions; the Brazilian government has been publicly critical of Washington's posture toward the vote.

The timing is unusual. Suspending consular operations — not merely issuing a travel advisory — days before a national election sends a signal about perceived instability or threat levels in a major Western Hemisphere democracy at a moment of sharp political polarization between Lula and Bolsonaro's camp.
sections.whyItMatters: Brazil is the largest economy in Latin America and a pivotal non-aligned voice. If a US-Brazil relationship already strained by tariffs and political friction now includes embassy closures around an election, Washington risks being seen as intervening in — or writing off — a hemisphere election at exactly the wrong moment.

bottomLine: Three separate theaters moved toward or into open conflict today — North Korea answered Seoul's apology demand with a medium-range missile; Ethiopia and Eritrea severed all diplomatic ties as Ethiopian-allied forces closed on Mekelle; and Saudi Arabia prepared a 100,000-troop offensive to wrench the Bab al-Mandeb from the Houthis with Washington declining to join. None of these has a functioning off-ramp, and all three are drawing in regional partners with their own agendas. The common thread is that the post-Cold War habit of outsourcing crisis management to the US is failing: in the Red Sea, the Gulf, the Horn and Asia, local powers are now making unilateral moves while Washington is stretched. Meanwhile Europe's rearmament plans met their first domestic reversal in Italy, and the US-Iran Hormuz framework remains unresolved. Watch whether the Saudi Yemen offensive actually launches in the coming weeks, and whether North Korea follows its missile with a nuclear or ICBM test.
